title: RoboPhD: Self-Improving Text-to-SQL Through Autonomous Agent Evolution
mutable_substrate: A domain-specific Text-to-SQL agent package: deterministic Python database-analysis tools under tools/*.py plus Markdown SQL-generation instructions in eval_instructions.md. Model weights, evaluator, ELO rule, sampling protocol, runtime verifier, and the main evolution-strategy prompt remain fixed.
optimization_operator: Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5 or Opus 4.5 performs LLM-guided cross-pollination of complementary parent artifacts, informed by error reports and ratings, then applies same-session Deep Focus testing and revision (default one prior-iteration round).
feedback_selection: BIRD execution accuracy on a new 150-question sample per standard iteration (five training databases, 30 questions each) is decomposed into pairwise win/tie/loss outcomes for persistent ELO updates with K=32. The previous sample winner, a new candidate, and a random top-two ELO incumbent normally form the next contest; late rounds allocate 15% to under-tested challengers and 15% to random re-evaluation.
archive_memory: A persistent population stores candidate code and prompts, ELO ratings, accuracy histories, detailed error-analysis reports, and reasoning.md design traces. Cross-pollination can draw from multiple highly rated candidates; a Claude Code session retains context during one candidate's creation and Deep Focus refinement, not across the full outer run.
validation_strategy: Evolution and selection use repeatedly resampled BIRD training tasks. Generalization is checked on 11 BIRD development databases across Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus 4.5, followed by an official BIRD test evaluation by the benchmark team for two submitted Opus configurations. The paper reports no replicate evolutionary runs, confidence intervals, dedicated held-out selection split, or controlled component ablations.
adaptation_mode: Offline domain-specific evolution followed by static deployment. The final Python analyzer runs once per database and its cached analysis plus fixed instructions support online SQL generation and self-verification; no runtime self-modification or continual adaptation occurs.
benchmarks: BIRD training set: 69 databases and approximately 6,600 questions
Official BIRD test set with simple, moderate, and challenging breakdowns
principal_results: BIRD development accuracy improves from 69.0% to 71.3% for Claude Opus 4.5 (+2.3 points), from 65.7% to 69.2% for Sonnet 4.5 (+3.5), and from 57.2% to 66.1% for Haiku 4.5 (+8.9).
Evolved Haiku reaches 66.1% at 0.51 cents per query versus naive Sonnet at 65.7% and 0.56 cents; evolved Sonnet reaches 69.2% at 0.87 cents versus naive Opus at 69.0% and 1.61 cents.

Official BIRD test accuracy with Opus 4.5 rises from 72.16% to 73.67% (+1.51), with changes of -0.32 on simple, +1.80 on moderate, and +7.02 on challenging questions; the result ranked 16th in December 2025.

The iteration-18 champion combines three iteration-17 parents at 76% sampled training accuracy and uses size-adaptive database analysis to avoid prior 0% context-overflow failures under a 200K-token limit.
The artifact grows from about 70 lines to roughly 1,500 lines: an approximately 1,000-line Python analyzer and 527-line SQL instruction file.
limitations: One reported stochastic evolutionary trajectory provides no run-to-run variance, confidence intervals, random-seed analysis, or statistical significance tests.
No quantitative ablations isolate ELO, cross-pollination, Deep Focus depth, late-stage challenger rounds, universal verification, tool-only analysis, or individual champion features.
Repeated adaptive use of the same 69-database training pool for mutation, refinement, rating, and winner selection can overfit the pool despite changing per-iteration samples.
The claimed inverse scaling of evolutionary benefit is observational across three same-vendor Claude tiers, while evolution itself uses Haiku for SQL generation.
A scalar ELO rating discards win margins, uncertainty, and domain-specific non-transitive specialization.
Cost accounting excludes Claude Code subscription quota, local compute, engineering, security review, and failed trajectories; within each model tier the evolved artifact costs more per query.
Only BIRD, SQLite, and Claude 4.5 models are evaluated, so cross-domain, cross-model, schema-drift, and production generalization remain unknown.
safety_controls: Evolution runs use process isolation and filesystem permissions for unreviewed generated code.
Prompts and outputs are constrained to benchmark-permitted schemas, evidence, and allowed literature, with no ground-truth SQL or private test questions exposed to agents.
Key prompt and output logs are retained for audit, and the official BIRD team evaluated two submitted test configurations.

The paper recommends sandboxing, network isolation, least privilege, and security review for production, but does not empirically test adversarial schemas, exfiltration, prompt injection, or sensitive-data controls.

explicit_predecessors.name: TextGrad
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit lineage: RoboPhD likens its detailed prior-agent error reports to textual gradients that an LLM can turn into corrective changes.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Section 2.1 explicitly names TextGrad and says RoboPhD's error feedback is similar to text gradients, while leaving incorporation decisions to the Evolution Agent.

explicit_predecessors.name: APE, OPRO, DSPy, and ACE
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit comparison and methodological broadening: prior systems optimize prompts, whereas RoboPhD evolves prompts together with executable database-analysis tools.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Section 2.1 groups these systems under prompt optimization and contrasts their mutable substrate with RoboPhD's complete agent artifacts.

explicit_predecessors.name: Neural architecture search and population-based training
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit methodological lineage: RoboPhD adapts evolutionary search from architectures and hyperparameters to natural-language-specified agent programs and tools.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Section 2.1 cites evolutionary neural architecture search, CMA-ES-style hyperparameter optimization, and population-based training immediately before stating that RoboPhD extends evolution to complete AI agents.

explicit_predecessors.name: ELO rating and Chatbot Arena
explicit_predecessors.relationship: Explicit methodological extension: a passive model-comparison rating is repurposed as an active evolutionary selection mechanism.
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Section 2.1 names chess ELO and Chatbot Arena, then claims RoboPhD introduces ELO for active evolutionary optimization; Section 3.2.5 specifies pairwise updates with K=32.

open_questions: Would repeated, seed-controlled runs reproduce the gain distribution and the same size-adaptive design?
How do ELO selection, raw held-out accuracy, uncertainty-aware ratings, quality-diversity search, and per-domain payoff models compare under matched budgets?
Which components causally matter: cross-pollination, Deep Focus, late-stage re-evaluation, deterministic analysis, universal verification, or particular champion features?
Can a held-out release-selection set prevent adaptive training-pool overfitting without making evolution prohibitively expensive?
Does the artifact transfer to other model providers, open models, SQL dialects, Spider 2.0, BIRD-Critic, schema drift, and non-database domains?
Can meta-evolution safely improve the hand-written strategy rather than merely add stochasticity after 30 or more rounds?
How should accuracy, security, maintainability, latency, context size, and total cost be optimized jointly before evolved code reaches production?
Can targeted LLM calls during database analysis outperform both deterministic tool-only and full LLM analysis at a controlled cost?
